verses.text: Now about that time, King Herod stretched out his hands to oppress some of the assembly.
He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.
When he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter also. This was during the days of unleavened bread.
When he had arrested him, he put him in prison, and delivered him to four squads of four soldiers each to guard him, intending to bring him out to the people after the Passover.
Peter therefore was kept in the prison, but constant prayer was made by the assembly to God for him.
The same night when Herod was about to bring him out, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains. Guards in front of the door kept the prison.
And behold, an angel of the Lord stood by him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side, and woke him up, saying, “Stand up quickly!” His chains fell off from his hands.
The angel said to him, “Get dressed and put on your sandals.” He did so. He said to him, “Put on your cloak, and follow me.”
And he went out and followed him. He didn’t know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he saw a vision.

When they were past the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate that leads into the city, which opened to them by itself. They went out, and went down one street, and immediately the angel departed from him.
When Peter had come to himself, he said, “Now I truly know that the Lord has sent out his angel and delivered me out of the hand of Herod, and from everything the Jewish people were expecting.”
Thinking about that, he came to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was called Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying.
When Peter knocked at the door of the gate, a maid named Rhoda came to answer.
When she recognized Peter’s voice, she didn’t open the gate for joy, but ran in, and reported that Peter was standing in front of the gate.
They said to her, “You are crazy!” But she insisted that it was so. They said, “It is his angel.”
But Peter continued knocking. When they had opened, they saw him, and were amazed.

But he, beckoning to them with his hand to be silent, declared to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. He said, “Tell these things to James, and to the brothers.” Then he departed, and went to another place.
Now as soon as it was day, there was no small stir among the soldiers about what had become of Peter.
When Herod had sought for him, and didn’t find him, he examined the guards, and commanded that they should be put to death. He went down from Judea to Caesarea, and stayed there.

Now Herod was very angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon. They came with one accord to him, and, having made Blastus, the king’s personal aide, their friend, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food.
On an appointed day, Herod dressed himself in royal clothing, sat on the throne, and gave a speech to them.
The people shouted, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!”
Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and died.
But the word of God grew and multiplied.
Barnabas and Saul returned to  Jerusalem, when they had fulfilled their service, also taking with them John who was called Mark.

footnotes.content: Herod is moving against the church now—not reasoned debate, but open cruelty. I notice how quickly a ruler's hand can turn when fear and pride meet. The church is learning what it means to suffer for the name, not in theory but in blood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: James—John's brother, one of the first to leave everything and follow Jesus—is the first apostle to drink the cup of martyrdom. Luke names him plainly: killed by the sword. The first of the Twelve to complete the way of the cross.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Herod sees that killing James pleased the crowd, and fear of men becomes his compass. He arrests Peter next, calculating: one more death will buy him favor. How easily we lose our way when we measure truth by applause.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sixteen soldiers—four squads—guarding one old fisherman. The machinery of Rome rolls out in full measure, as if Peter's frail body could escape without walls and chains and eyes. The mighty always overestimate what chains can hold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: While Peter sits locked in a cell, the assembly prays—not for rescue, but constant prayer, steady as breath. This is the church's real strength: not defense or debate, but staying on her knees before the throne that all earthly rulers answer to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter sleeps between two soldiers, bound with chains, and he is at peace. I think about that—sleeping like a child while death waits on the other side of morning. His rest is a quiet witness: the Lord is keeper.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The angel strikes Peter's side—a touch to wake him from sleep into freedom, chains falling like morning dew. Light blazes in the dark cell, and Peter sees: help has come, not from Rome or the wise, but from the Lord's own hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Get dressed. Put on your sandals. Put on your cloak. Follow me." Every word is tender and clear—the angel makes ready the man for the road, clothes him, and shows him the way. The Lord doesn't abandon us naked to confusion; He equips and directs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter thinks he's dreaming, that it's a vision—his mind struggles to believe what his feet are walking out. Grace often comes too bright for us to see clearly at first. We wake only when we step into the light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The iron gate opens of itself, and they pass guard after guard unseen. Iron gates, locked and watched—all of it yields to the Lord's gentle word. Then the angel leaves, and Peter stands alone on the street, free.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter comes to himself, and the truth breaks over him like the morning sun: the Lord sent His angel. He is delivered from Herod's hand and from the very doom the people expected for him. When we wake to God's mercy, everything changes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter walks to the house of Mary, mother of John Mark—a mother's home becomes a prayer-room, a place where the church gathers to cry out for one of their own. Many hands were lifted in prayer when the angel's hand reached into the cell.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rhoda hears a knock at the gate—just a knock—and recognizes Peter's voice. Such a small thing, yet it carries the whole joy of the resurrection: the dead come back to us, and we know them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rhoda's joy breaks all protocol: she doesn't open the gate, but runs inside to tell them. Her heart outpaces her head; she can't contain the news. When good comes suddenly, we forget ourselves and shout for gladness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They call her mad, caught between hope and disbelief. Even when they say "It must be his angel," they don't quite trust that the Lord would break chains and walls for them. We live more by our fears than by the God we've seen deliver.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter keeps knocking—patient, real, undeniable. When they finally open the door and see him, amazement fills the room. Sometimes faith waits at the gate until we're ready to believe what we're seeing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter gestures for silence—a hand raised, a quiet word. He tells them what the Lord has done, and sends word to James (now the leader in Jerusalem, Peter's anchor) and the brothers. Then he departs to another place, disappearing again into the Lord's care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Morning comes, and the soldiers wake to terror: their prisoner is gone. No commotion, no broken chains—just an empty cell. When the Lord moves, the earth itself seems to conspire for grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Herod cannot find Peter, so he executes the very soldiers who guarded him—innocent blood spilled for the rage of a king. This is what tyranny does when mercy escapes its grasp: it turns on its own. Herod then flees to Caesarea, never knowing that his defeat was set in stone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tyre and Sidon come to Herod seeking peace, because they depend on his land for food—a political matter of grain and trade. They work through Blastus, the king's personal aide, to arrange an audience. The stage is set for pride to meet its reckoning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Herod dresses in royal clothing and sits on the throne to address them. He is adorned, elevated, resplendent—a king among his people, ready to dispense favor or judgment as he wills.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The voice of a god, and not of a man!" they cry. Flattery is the incense of power, and Herod drinks it in. He does not rebuke them; he does not speak the name of the true God. His silence is his sin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An angel of the Lord strikes him—the same angels who freed Peter now execute the king who ordered His servant's death. Herod is eaten by worms and dies because he stole the Lord's glory and kept it for himself. Pride goes before destruction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But the word of God grew and multiplied. After chains and crosses, after tyrants and sword-strokes, the gospel spreads—not held back by walls or death, not diminished by persecution. Readers today hear an echo: even now, the word grows where the church is faithful, and no earthly power can finally stop it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Barnabas and Saul return to Jerusalem, their service completed, bringing young Mark with them. The work moves on, the hands change, and the Lord continues. In His kingdom, no one is indispensable, yet each of us is called.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
